title: Every Part Named
bigQuestion: How do two threads, one above the fabric and one below, lock together thousands of times a minute without a single hand touching them?

story.title: The Machine That Would Not Behave
story.kicker: Priya's machine jammed three times in ten minutes. The fix was not in the machine at all.
paragraphs: On the first day at the sewing machines, Ms. Delgado gave each student a scrap of muslin and one instruction: "Sew a straight line from one edge to the other." Priya sat at machine number six, pressed the foot pedal, and the machine roared for about two seconds. Then it stopped with a thunk. Underneath the fabric was a tangle of thread the size of a grape.

She cut the fabric free, pulled the tangle out of the bobbin area with tweezers, and tried again. Same thing. The top of the seam looked almost fine, but the underside was a nest of loose loops. A boy at machine five leaned over. "Your tension is broken," he said. "Turn the dial up." Priya turned the dial from 4 to 7. The third try jammed just like the first two.

Ms. Delgado came over, looked at the underside, and did not touch the tension dial. "Loops on the bottom mean the top thread is loose," she said. "Let's see how you threaded it." She raised the presser foot, pulled the top thread all the way out, and had Priya do it again: spool pin, thread guide, down to the tension discs, up and through the take-up lever, down to the needle. "Presser foot up when you thread. That opens the discs so the thread can drop in between them."

Priya had threaded with the presser foot down. The thread had never gone between the tension discs at all. It had just lain on top of them, with no tension on it whatsoever. The dial setting had never mattered, because the thread never touched the dial. Ms. Delgado set the tension back to 4 and lowered the foot.

The fourth line of stitching came out clean on both sides: small, even, locked in the middle of the fabric. Priya held it up to the light and could not tell the top from the bottom. "The machine was fine the whole time," Ms. Delgado said. "Before you touch a dial, check the path. It is almost always the path."
story.think: Priya's first fix was to turn the tension dial up. Why could that never have fixed the problem, and what should she have checked first?

sections.title: The Parts and What They Do

lessons.title: Touring the Machine
lessons.mainIdea: A sewing machine has about a dozen named parts, and you cannot thread it, fix it or read its manual until you know where each one is.
reading: Sit in front of a machine with it turned off and unplugged. Start at the top right. The *spool pin* is the post the thread spool sits on. Next to it is the *bobbin winder*, a small spindle that spins an empty bobbin to fill it with thread. On the right side is the *hand wheel*, a large wheel you turn toward yourself to raise or lower the needle by hand. Never turn it away from you; that can pull the thread out of the needle and tangle it.

Now follow the front of the machine down. Thread guides are small hooks or slots that keep the thread on its path. The tension discs are two metal plates that pinch the thread; a dial sets how hard they pinch. The *take-up lever* is a metal arm that rises and falls with every stitch. It pulls thread up to tighten each stitch. At the bottom is the needle, held by a needle clamp screw, and the *presser foot*, a small metal foot that holds the fabric flat against the bed.

Under the presser foot is the throat plate, a metal plate with a hole for the needle and lines marked for seam widths. Through slots in the plate come the *feed dogs*, rows of small metal teeth that move the fabric forward one stitch at a time. Below all of that, behind a small door, is the bobbin, a little spool of thread that supplies the bottom half of every stitch.

On the front or side are the controls: stitch selector, stitch length dial, stitch width dial and a reverse lever or button. On the floor is the foot pedal, which is the machine's gas pedal. Press lightly and it sews slowly; press hard and it races. Touch each part and say its name out loud before you go on. On a practical test, the first question is usually a diagram with blank labels.

words.d: the post on top of the machine that holds the spool of thread
the large wheel on the right side, turned toward you to move the needle by hand
the metal arm that rises and falls with each stitch, pulling the top thread tight
the small metal foot that holds fabric flat against the feed dogs while you sew
rows of metal teeth under the presser foot that move the fabric forward one stitch at a time

look.title: Blank Diagram, Ten Labels
look.text: Picture the machine from the front. A post on top with a spool on it. A large wheel on the right end. A metal arm near the top left that moves up and down. A dial with numbers 0 to 9. A thin steel pin at the bottom center. A small metal foot below it. A flat plate with a hole and marked lines. Teeth showing through slots in the plate. A little door below the plate. A pedal on the floor.
look.prompt: Name each of the ten parts in order, and say what happens if the wheel is turned the wrong way.

check.q: Which part moves the fabric forward under the needle?
check.why: The feed dogs are the teeth under the presser foot; they grip the fabric and move it forward one stitch at a time.

check.q: Which direction do you turn the hand wheel?
choices: Either way, it does not matter
Only while the pedal is pressed
check.why: The hand wheel always turns toward you. Turning it away can pull the thread out of the needle and cause a jam.

check.q: A student wants to sew slowly while learning. What controls the speed?
choices: How hard the foot pedal is pressed
check.why: The foot pedal works like a gas pedal. Light pressure sews slowly; more pressure sews faster.

lessons.title: Needle Types and Sizes
lessons.mainIdea: The needle must match the fabric: a ballpoint for knits, a universal for most wovens, a heavy needle for denim, and a fresh one for every project.
reading: Look closely at a machine needle. It has a flat side on the shank at the top, a long groove down the front, a scarf (a scooped-out spot) on the back just above the eye, and a point. The flat side faces the back of the machine on most home machines, so the needle can only go in one way. The eye is near the point, not at the top like a hand needle, because the machine pushes the thread down through the fabric instead of pulling it.

Needles come in types by point shape. A *universal* needle has a slightly rounded point and handles most woven cottons and blends. A *ballpoint* needle has a rounder tip that slides between the loops of a knit fabric instead of piercing and cutting them; use it for T-shirt jersey and fleece. A stretch needle is for very stretchy fabric like swimwear. A denim or jeans needle has a strong, sharp point for thick layers. A microtex or sharp needle makes a fine straight hole in silky fabric.

Needles also come in sizes, written as two numbers such as 80/12 or 90/14. The first number is the European size and the second the American; both get bigger as the needle gets thicker. A 70/10 suits light cotton, an 80/12 is the everyday size for medium fabric, and a 100/16 handles denim. A needle that is too thin for the fabric bends and breaks; one that is too thick leaves visible holes.

Needles dull with use, and a dull needle skips stitches and punches instead of piercing. Many sewers change the needle at the start of every project or after about eight hours of sewing. To change it, turn the machine off, loosen the needle clamp screw, pull the old needle down and out, push the new one up as far as it will go with the flat side to the back, and tighten the screw. Drop the old needle into a lidded container, never a bare trash can.

words.d: a machine needle with a slightly rounded point that suits most woven fabrics
a needle with a rounded tip that slips between knit loops instead of cutting them
the thickness of a needle, written as two numbers such as 80/12; bigger numbers are thicker
the scooped-out spot on the back of a machine needle above the eye, where the hook catches the thread

look.title: Common Needle Sizes and Their Fabrics (a typical guide)
look.cite: typical home-sewing needle guide; check your machine manual and needle package
look.prompt: A student has heavy denim and only a 70/10 needle. What is likely to happen, and what size should they get?

check.q: Which needle should you use for a stretchy T-shirt knit?
check.why: A ballpoint needle slides between knit loops instead of cutting them, so the fabric does not get runs or holes.

check.q: What does a bigger needle number, like 100/16 instead of 70/10, mean?
check.why: Both numbers grow as the needle gets thicker. A 100/16 is a heavy needle for denim; a 70/10 is thin, for light fabric.

check.q: When you insert a new needle on a home machine, which way does the flat side of the shank face?
choices: Toward the back of the machine
check.why: The flat side faces the back on most home machines, so the needle seats correctly and the scarf faces the hook.

lessons.title: Reading the Manual
lessons.mainIdea: Every machine is a little different, and the manual is where the threading diagram, the bobbin type and the needle position for your machine actually live.
reading: Two machines side by side in a classroom can thread differently, take different bobbins and put the stitch length on a different dial. That is why the first tool for any machine is its *manual*. If the paper copy is lost, the model number is printed on a plate on the back or bottom of the machine, and the maker usually posts the manual online for free. Print the threading diagram and tape it to the table.

Open the manual and find four things before you sew. First, the threading diagram, drawn as numbered arrows from the spool to the needle. Second, the bobbin section: does the machine take a drop-in bobbin from the top, or a front-loading bobbin in a metal *bobbin case*? Third, the needle-threading direction: front to back on most machines, but some thread side to side. Fourth, the normal tension setting, often 4 on a dial that runs 0 to 9.

The manual also has a troubleshooting table near the back. It lists the problem in one column (thread breaks, fabric will not feed, skipped stitches) and the likely causes in the other. Almost every cause is one of four things: threading, needle, bobbin, or lint. Read that table once now, so that when the machine acts up, you know the list exists.

Class machines get shared, so the manual is also the record of what the machine can do. Note the stitches it offers, the widest zigzag it can make, and what presser feet came with it. A zipper foot or a buttonhole foot in the accessory box is useless if nobody knows it is there.

words.d: the maker's booklet for one model of machine, with its threading diagram and troubleshooting table
the small metal holder a bobbin sits in on a front-loading machine; it sets the bobbin thread tension
a bobbin that sits in a clear-lidded well on top of the machine bed, in front of the needle

look.title: Four Machines, Four Answers
look.text: Machine A: front-loading bobbin case, threads front to back. Machine B: drop-in bobbin, threads front to back. Machine C: drop-in bobbin, threads left to right. Machine D: front-loading, tension dial normal at 3 instead of 4. A student who learned on Machine B sits down at Machine C and threads the needle front to back.
look.prompt: What will happen on Machine C, and what one page of the manual would have prevented it?

check.q: Where is the model number of a sewing machine usually found?
choices: On a plate on the back or bottom of the machine
check.why: The model plate is on the back or underside. With the model number you can find the manual online.

check.q: Which part of the manual should you check when the thread keeps breaking?
check.why: The troubleshooting table lists each problem with its likely causes, which are usually threading, needle, bobbin or lint.

check.q: A machine's bobbin sits under a clear lid in front of the needle. What kind of bobbin system is that?
check.why: A drop-in bobbin sits in a well on top of the bed under a clear plate. Front-loading bobbins go in a metal case behind a door.

lessons.title: The Top Thread Path
lessons.mainIdea: The top thread follows one fixed path from spool to needle, and it only works if the presser foot is up when you thread it.
reading: Turn the machine off. Raise the presser foot with the lever behind it. This matters more than any other step: raising the foot opens the tension discs so the thread can slip between them. Turn the hand wheel toward you until the take-up lever is at its highest point, where you can see it through the slot. Now put the spool on the spool pin with the thread coming off in the direction the manual shows, and cap it with the spool holder if the machine has one.

Pull the thread to the left along the top of the machine and into the first thread guide. Bring it down the front channel, around the bottom, and back up. On the way down it passes between the tension discs; you may feel a tiny click as it seats. At the top of the channel it goes right to left through the eye of the take-up lever. If you miss the take-up lever, every stitch will be loose. Then bring it straight down through the lower thread guides to the needle.

Thread the needle from front to back on most machines, and pull about six inches of thread out behind the presser foot. Many machines have a built-in needle threader: a tiny hook that swings through the eye, catches the thread, and pulls it back through. Now lower the presser foot. Turn the hand wheel one full turn toward you, and the needle thread will catch the bobbin thread and pull a loop of it up through the throat plate.

Check your work with a tug test. With the presser foot up, the thread should pull freely. Lower the foot and pull again; there should be firm drag. If it pulls freely with the foot down, the thread is not between the discs. Pull it out and rethread. Threading takes thirty seconds when it becomes a habit, and it prevents most of the jams a beginner ever sees.

words.d: two metal plates that pinch the top thread; the presser foot lever opens them for threading
a hook or slot that holds the thread on its path between the spool and the needle
a small built-in hook that pushes through the needle eye, catches the thread and pulls it back

look.title: Put the Path in Order
look.text: Six steps, out of order: (a) through the eye of the take-up lever; (b) raise the presser foot and put the take-up lever at its highest point; (c) through the needle eye, front to back; (d) into the first thread guide on top; (e) down between the tension discs; (f) spool on the spool pin.
look.prompt: Write the letters in the right order, and say which single step, if skipped, leaves the thread with no tension at all.

check.q: Why must the presser foot be UP when you thread the top of the machine?
choices: So the needle can move freely
So the tension discs open and the thread can seat between them
So the bobbin can drop in
check.why: Raising the presser foot opens the tension discs. With the foot down the discs are closed and the thread lies on top of them with no tension.

check.q: A seam has good stitches for two inches and then every stitch is loose. The student threaded the machine with the foot up, but skipped one part. Which part?
check.why: The take-up lever pulls each stitch tight. If the thread is not through its eye, the stitches stay loose.

check.q: What does a correct tug test feel like with the presser foot down?
choices: The thread pulls freely with no drag
The thread will not move at all
The thread pulls with firm, even drag
check.why: With the foot down the discs are closed, so a correctly seated thread pulls with steady drag. Free pulling means it missed the discs.

lessons.title: Winding a Bobbin
lessons.mainIdea: A bobbin must be wound evenly, at a steady speed, with the same thread as the top, or the stitch underneath will never be right.
reading: A *bobbin* is a small flat spool that holds the bottom thread. Use an empty bobbin made for your machine; bobbins look alike but differ by a millimeter, and the wrong one jams or rattles. Use the same thread as the top for ordinary seams. Put the spool on the spool pin, run the thread through the bobbin winder guide (often a small disc on top of the machine), and pass the end through the hole in the bobbin from the inside out.

Push the bobbin onto the bobbin winder spindle and click the spindle to the right, which disengages the needle so it will not move while you wind. On older machines you loosen the hand wheel's inner knob instead. Hold the thread tail up, press the pedal slowly for a few turns so the thread catches, stop, and trim the tail close to the bobbin. Then press the pedal at a steady, medium speed and let the machine fill the bobbin. Most machines stop by themselves when it is full.

Watch the bobbin as it fills. The thread should lie in smooth, even layers. If it piles up on one side, the thread is not through the winder guide correctly; stop and fix it. Do not overfill; thread should not bulge past the rim. Cut the thread, click the spindle back to the left, and the needle is connected again. Turn the hand wheel a half turn to make sure.

Two common mistakes: winding on top of thread already on the bobbin, which makes uneven tension and a bird's nest underneath, and winding at a jerky speed, which stretches some layers tighter than others. Keep a few extra bobbins wound in the colors you use most; running out mid-seam is a nuisance, not a disaster, but it always happens at the worst moment.

words.d: the small flat spool under the throat plate that supplies the bottom thread of every stitch
the spindle on top of the machine that spins an empty bobbin to fill it with thread
a tangle of loose thread under the fabric, usually from threading or bobbin mistakes

look.title: A Bobbin That Looks Wrong
look.text: A student holds up a freshly wound bobbin. The thread is piled high on the left rim and thin on the right, and there is a loose loop hanging off. Under the new thread you can see a layer of blue thread from last week. The student says it will probably work.
look.prompt: Name the two winding mistakes you can see, and say what each one will do to the stitch on the underside of the fabric.

check.q: Before winding a bobbin, why do you click the winder spindle to the right?
choices: To disengage the needle so it does not move while you wind
check.why: Moving the spindle into winding position disconnects the needle. Otherwise the needle stitches away while you wind.

check.q: A wound bobbin has thread piled on one side and thin on the other. What went wrong?
choices: The thread was not seated in the winder guide
The pedal was pressed too softly
check.why: The winder guide feeds the thread onto the bobbin evenly. If the thread misses it, the layers pile up unevenly.

check.q: What is the safest rule about the bobbin you choose?
choices: Use the biggest one that fits
Use the bobbin made for your machine model
Use a metal bobbin in every machine
check.why: Bobbins differ by a millimeter or so between models. A wrong-size bobbin rattles, jams or throws the tension off.

lessons.title: Inserting the Bobbin
lessons.mainIdea: The bobbin must sit in its case or well with the thread coming off in the direction the manual shows, then be pulled through its own tension spring and up through the plate.
reading: There are two systems. For a *drop-in* machine, slide off the clear cover in front of the needle. Hold the bobbin so the thread comes off in the direction the diagram on the cover shows, usually counterclockwise, like a letter P when you look at it. Drop it into the well, then pull the thread tail into the slot and along the guide path marked by arrows, which slides it under a small tension spring. Leave a few inches of tail and replace the cover.

For a *front-loading* machine, open the door below the needle and pull out the bobbin case by its little hinged latch. Hold the case in your left hand with the open side up and drop the bobbin in so the thread comes off in the direction the manual shows. Pull the thread into the slit on the side of the case and under the flat tension spring until it clicks out the end. Hold the latch open, push the case onto the center pin until it clicks, and let go of the latch.

Now bring the bobbin thread up. Hold the top thread loosely in your left hand. Turn the hand wheel one full turn toward you. The needle goes down, catches the bobbin thread and lifts a loop of it. Tug the top thread and the loop comes through the hole in the throat plate. Pull both tails out and lay them back under the presser foot, toward the rear. Starting a seam with the tails held behind the foot stops the first stitch from pulling down into the plate.

If the bobbin is put in backward, the thread unwinds the wrong way against its spring and the bottom stitches come out loose or the thread breaks. If the thread never went under the bobbin tension spring, there is no bottom tension at all, and loops of top thread show on the underside. Both look like tension problems. Both are really bobbin problems, and both take twenty seconds to fix.

words.d: a bobbin system where the bobbin drops into a well on top of the bed under a clear cover
a bobbin system where the bobbin sits in a removable metal case behind a door below the needle
the flat spring on the bobbin case or well that the bottom thread must pass under to get its tension

look.title: Two Bobbins, One Right
look.text: Two drop-in machines sit side by side. In machine one the bobbin thread comes off counterclockwise, matching the arrow on the cover, and runs through the slot under the spring. In machine two the bobbin was dropped in flipped over, so the thread comes off clockwise, and the tail was left lying loose on top of the bobbin.
look.prompt: Predict what the underside of the first seam will look like on machine two, and list the two fixes in order.

check.q: After dropping in the bobbin, why do you pull the thread through the slot along the arrows?
choices: To seat the thread under the bobbin tension spring
check.why: The slot guides the thread under the bobbin's flat tension spring. Without that, the bottom thread has no tension.

check.q: How do you bring the bobbin thread up through the throat plate?
choices: Turn the hand wheel one full turn toward you while holding the top thread
Pull it up with tweezers through the needle hole
Wind the bobbin with the cover off
check.why: One turn of the hand wheel sends the needle down to catch the bobbin thread and lift a loop. A tug on the top thread pulls it through.

check.q: Where should both thread tails be before you start sewing?
choices: Pulled back under and behind the presser foot
Cut off flush with the plate
check.why: Tails laid toward the rear under the foot stop the first stitch from pulling the thread down into the plate.

lessons.title: The Lockstitch, Step by Step
lessons.mainIdea: A lockstitch forms when the needle carries the top thread down, a hook loops it around the bobbin thread, and the take-up lever pulls the two threads tight so they lock inside the fabric.
reading: A home sewing machine makes a *lockstitch*. It is nothing like hand sewing, where one thread goes in and out. Here two threads never actually pass through each other's spools; they twist around each other once per stitch and lock in the middle of the fabric. Turn the hand wheel slowly toward you with the bobbin cover off and you can watch the whole thing happen.

Step one: the needle pushes the top thread down through the fabric and through the hole in the throat plate. Step two: the needle starts back up. Because the thread drags a little against the fabric, a small loop of top thread bulges out on the scarf side of the needle. Step three: the *hook*, a curved metal point spinning around the bobbin, catches that loop and carries it all the way around the bobbin case, so the loop now wraps around the bobbin thread.

Step four: the take-up lever rises fast and yanks the slack out of the top thread. That pulls the twist of the two threads up into the layers of fabric. At the same time the feed dogs push the fabric forward one stitch length. Step five: the needle comes down again and the cycle repeats. A machine at full speed can do this several hundred times a minute, and each stitch is locked by the one before it.

This is why the scarf on the needle matters and why the needle must be in the right way around: the hook has to pass right behind the eye to catch the loop. It is also why a bent or dull needle skips stitches. If the loop forms in the wrong place, the hook misses it, and no stitch forms for that beat. Understanding the cycle turns most machine problems from mysteries into checklists.

words.d: the machine stitch made by the top thread looping around the bobbin thread and locking in the fabric
the curved point that spins around the bobbin and catches the loop of top thread on each stitch
a beat where the hook misses the loop and no stitch forms, leaving a long gap in the seam

look.title: Watch One Stitch Form
look.text: With the bobbin cover off, a student turns the hand wheel toward herself very slowly and describes what she sees: the needle goes down through a scrap. As it starts to rise, a small loop of thread bulges out behind the needle. A curved point sweeps past and takes the loop around the bobbin. Then the arm at the top jerks up and the loop disappears into the fabric.
look.prompt: Name the part doing the work at each of the four moments, and explain why turning the wheel away from her would break the cycle.

check.q: Which part catches the loop of top thread and carries it around the bobbin?
check.why: The hook is the curved point that spins around the bobbin. It catches the loop that forms behind the rising needle.

check.q: What does the take-up lever do right after the loop goes around the bobbin?
choices: Pulls the slack out so the two threads lock inside the fabric
check.why: The take-up lever rises and pulls the top thread tight, drawing the twist of the two threads up into the fabric layers.

check.q: Why does a bent needle cause skipped stitches?
choices: The loop forms in the wrong place and the hook misses it
check.why: The hook must pass right behind the needle's scarf to catch the loop. A bent needle puts the loop out of reach.

lessons.title: Stitch Length and Width
lessons.mainIdea: Stitch length sets how far the fabric moves per stitch and width sets how far the needle swings sideways; 2.5 mm straight is the everyday setting.
reading: The *stitch length* dial controls the feed dogs. A higher number moves the fabric farther between needle strikes, so each stitch is longer. Most machines mark length in millimeters, from 0 to 4 or 5. Some older machines use stitches per inch instead, where a bigger number means shorter stitches. For ordinary seams in medium fabric, set 2.5 mm, which is about 10 to 12 stitches per inch. Set the dial before you sew; changing it mid-seam leaves a visible step in the stitching.

Use a long stitch, 4 to 5 mm, for *basting*: a temporary seam you will pull out later, or gathering, where you pull the bobbin thread to draw the fabric up into small folds. Long stitches are easy to remove. Use a shorter stitch, about 2 mm, for lightweight fabric and curves, where short stitches follow the shape better. Very short stitches, under 1 mm, are hard to rip out and can chew the fabric.

The *stitch width* dial controls how far the needle swings from side to side. On a straight stitch the width is zero and the needle goes straight up and down. Turn the width up and the machine sews a *zigzag*. A width of about 3 mm with a length of 2 mm gives a medium zigzag good for finishing a raw edge. A wide, very short zigzag becomes a satin stitch, the dense band used on appliqué and buttonholes.

Test every setting on a scrap of the same fabric first, doubled the way the seam will be. The scrap shows you whether the stitches lie flat, whether the fabric puckers, and whether the length looks right. Write the setting that worked on a sticky note and keep it with the project. A machine that is set right for one fabric is rarely right for the next.

words.d: how far the feed dogs move the fabric between stitches, usually in millimeters; 2.5 mm is standard
how far the needle swings sideways; zero for a straight stitch, more for zigzag
a temporary seam sewn with a long stitch, 4 to 5 mm, so it pulls out easily
a stitch where the needle swings side to side; used to finish edges and sew stretch seams

look.title: Stitch Length by Job (typical settings)
look.cite: typical home-machine settings; the machine manual and a test scrap decide the final number
look.prompt: A student basted a sleeve at 2.0 mm and now has to remove it. What went wrong, and which row should they have used?

check.q: What is a good stitch length for an ordinary seam in medium-weight cotton?
check.why: 2.5 mm, about 10 to 12 stitches per inch, is the everyday setting. Longer is for basting; much shorter is for dense stitching.

check.q: You need to gather a ruffle by pulling the bobbin thread. Which stitch length do you set?
check.why: Long stitches slide easily along the fabric when you pull the bobbin thread, and they pull out cleanly afterward.

check.q: Which dial do you turn to change a straight stitch into a zigzag?
check.why: Width controls the needle's side-to-side swing. At zero the needle goes straight; turning it up makes a zigzag.

lessons.title: Reading the Tension
lessons.mainIdea: A balanced stitch locks in the middle of the fabric; loops on the bottom mean the top is too loose, and bobbin thread showing on top means the top is too tight.
reading: *Tension* is how hard each thread is held back as it feeds. The top thread's tension comes from the discs and the dial; the bobbin thread's comes from the small spring on the case or well. When the two match, the twist where the threads lock sits in the middle of the fabric layers, and the seam looks the same on both sides. To learn to read tension, sew a test line with a different color in the bobbin than on top.

Look at the underside. If you see loops or straight runs of the top color lying on the bottom, the top thread is too *loose*: it is being pulled all the way through to the underside. Turn the top tension dial to a higher number, one step at a time, and test again. If instead the bobbin color shows in dots along the top of the seam, the top thread is too *tight*: it is dragging the bobbin thread up. Turn the dial to a lower number.

Before you touch the dial, though, check the path. In most classrooms, nine out of ten "tension problems" are a top thread that missed the discs or the take-up lever, a bobbin inserted backward, or a bobbin thread that never went under its spring. Rethread top and bobbin with the presser foot up and test again. Only if a correctly threaded machine still stitches unevenly do you change the dial. Adjusting the bobbin spring is a last resort and is usually a teacher's job.

Some fabrics need a small change: thick layers may want slightly higher top tension, and very fine fabric slightly lower. Write down the dial number that gives a balanced stitch for each fabric, and always put the dial back to its normal setting, usually about 4, before you leave the machine for the next person.

words.d: how firmly the thread is held back as it feeds; top tension is set by the dial, bottom by the bobbin spring
a stitch where the two threads lock in the middle of the fabric and both sides look the same
too little top tension: the top thread shows as loops on the underside of the fabric
too much top tension: the bobbin thread is pulled up and shows as dots on the top side

look.title: Diagnose Three Seams
look.text: Three test seams, each sewn with red thread on top and blue in the bobbin. Seam 1: both sides show only their own color, flat and even. Seam 2: the underside has long red loops and the fabric puckers slightly. Seam 3: the top side shows a row of tiny blue dots, and the seam feels stiff and drawn up.
look.prompt: Say which seam is balanced, which is too loose on top, and which is too tight, and give the first thing to check for seams 2 and 3 before turning any dial.

check.q: Loops of top thread show on the underside of a seam. What does that tell you?
choices: The top thread is too loose
The top thread is too tight
check.why: When the top thread is pulled all the way through to the bottom and shows as loops, the top tension is too low (or the thread missed the discs).

check.q: What is the FIRST thing to do when a seam looks like a tension problem?
choices: Rethread top and bobbin with the presser foot up
check.why: Most tension symptoms are threading errors. Rethreading fixes them; the dial only matters once the path is right.

check.q: Dots of bobbin thread show on the top side of the seam. Which way do you turn the top tension dial?
choices: Lower, to loosen the top thread
Leave it; the bobbin is the problem
check.why: Bobbin thread on top means the top is pulling too hard. Lowering the top tension one step at a time brings the lock back to the middle.

lessons.title: Rules at the Machine
lessons.mainIdea: Fingers stay behind the needle, pins come out before the foot reaches them, and the machine is off whenever hands are near the needle.
reading: A sewing machine needle moves faster than you can pull away. That sets the first rule: keep your fingers at least an inch behind the presser foot, and guide the fabric from the sides, not the front. Never push fabric into the needle from in front of the foot. Let the feed dogs do the pulling; your hands only steer. Tie back long hair, remove dangling bracelets, and keep sleeves off the wheel.

Pins are the second hazard. Pin across the seam line, not along it, so the pin heads stick out to the right and are easy to grab. Pull each pin out just before the presser foot reaches it. Sewing over a pin can snap the needle, and a needle fragment flies at eye level. If the needle does break, turn the machine off, find every piece, and drop them in the sharps container.

Turn the machine off, or at least take your foot off the pedal, whenever your hands go near the needle: threading, changing the needle, changing the foot, clearing a jam. Never leave a foot resting on the pedal while you talk. Unplug the machine before you open it to clean. Keep the cord where nobody trips over it, and keep drinks off the sewing table, because a spill in a machine is a repair bill.

Work at a steady, moderate speed. Beginners who floor the pedal lose control of the seam and their hands drift toward the needle. If something goes wrong, stop; take your foot off the pedal before you lift your hands to investigate. Sewing is a calm skill. The machine only bites people who rush it.

words.d: a lidded, puncture-proof box for broken needles, bent pins and old blades
placing pins at a right angle to the seam line so they can be pulled out as the foot approaches
the habit of lifting your foot whenever your hands go near the needle

look.title: Spot the Hazards
look.text: A student sits at a machine with a water bottle on the table beside it. Her long hair hangs forward over the needle area. Pins run along the seam line, parallel to the edge, and she is sewing straight over them at full speed. Her left hand is in front of the presser foot, pushing the fabric toward the needle. A friend calls her name and she turns to talk with her foot still on the pedal.
look.prompt: List every unsafe thing in the scene, and for each say what could happen and what she should do instead.

check.q: Where should your fingers be while the machine is running?
choices: In front of the presser foot, pushing the fabric in
Behind and beside the presser foot, steering only
check.why: The feed dogs move the fabric. Hands stay behind and to the sides of the foot to steer, never in front of the needle.

check.q: Why should you pull out each pin before the foot reaches it?
choices: Pins slow down the feed dogs
Sewing over a pin can snap the needle and send a fragment flying
check.why: A needle that hits a pin can break, and the broken tip flies at eye height. Remove pins as the foot approaches.

check.q: What do you do before changing the needle or clearing a jam?
choices: Turn the machine off and take your foot off the pedal
check.why: The machine must not be able to start while hands are near the needle. Off, foot away from the pedal, then work.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Oiling
lessons.mainIdea: Lint builds up under the throat plate with every seam, and a machine brushed out and, if the manual says so, oiled regularly keeps stitching evenly for decades.
reading: Every stitch shaves a little fluff off the thread and the fabric, and it collects under the throat plate around the feed dogs and the bobbin. Enough *lint* there stops the bobbin thread from feeding smoothly and can make a well-threaded machine skip or jam. Cleaning is simple. Unplug the machine. Remove the needle and the presser foot, take out the bobbin, and unscrew or unclip the throat plate.

Use the small stiff brush that came with the machine to sweep lint out of the feed dogs and the bobbin area. Tweezers reach the stubborn bits. Do not blow into the machine; breath is damp and pushes lint deeper. Canned air pushes lint into the works too, so most manuals say brush, do not blow. Wipe the plate and the bobbin case with a dry cloth, put everything back, and turn the hand wheel a full turn by hand to make sure nothing binds.

Some machines need *oil*; many newer ones do not, so check the manual. If yours does, use only sewing machine oil, never household oil or cooking oil, which gum up. Put one drop on the spots the manual marks, usually in the hook race where the hook spins, then sew a few lines on a scrap to carry off any extra so it does not stain your project.

Cover the machine when it is not in use so dust does not settle into it. Change the needle regularly. Once a year or so, a sewing machine shop can service it fully. A well-cared-for machine from fifty years ago still sews a perfect seam; the ones that die are the ones nobody ever cleaned.

words.d: the fluff that thread and fabric shed while sewing; it gathers around the feed dogs and bobbin
the clear, light oil made for machines; household or cooking oils gum up the works
the track the hook spins in around the bobbin; the usual spot that takes one drop of oil

look.title: The Cleaning Kit and the Order
look.text: On the table: a small stiff brush, tweezers, a screwdriver for the throat plate, a dry cloth, a bottle of sewing machine oil, a can of compressed air, and a bottle of cooking spray somebody brought from home. Steps to arrange: brush the feed dogs; remove the throat plate; unplug the machine; take out the bobbin and needle; oil one drop if the manual says; sew on a scrap; reassemble.
look.prompt: Put the steps in order, and say which two items on the table should not be used on the machine and why.

check.q: What is the very first step before cleaning inside the machine?
check.why: Hands go near the needle and moving parts, so the machine must be unplugged, not just switched off.

check.q: Which tool should you use to remove lint from around the feed dogs?
choices: The small stiff brush that came with the machine
check.why: A brush lifts lint out. Blowing, by breath or by can, pushes lint and moisture deeper into the machine.

check.q: If a machine needs oil, which oil is correct?
check.why: Sewing machine oil is light and clear. Other oils thicken and gum up the works over time.

review.q: Which part pulls the top thread tight on every stitch?
review.why: The take-up lever rises with each stitch and pulls the slack out of the top thread so the lock sits in the fabric.

review.q: A student threads the machine with the presser foot down. What is the likely result?
choices: The thread misses the tension discs and loops appear underneath
review.why: The discs are closed with the foot down, so the thread never seats between them and has no tension. Loose loops form on the bottom.

review.q: Which needle size and type suits heavy denim?
review.why: Thick fabric needs a thick, sharp needle. A 100/16 denim needle pierces the layers without bending.

review.q: What does the hook do in forming a lockstitch?
choices: Catches the loop of top thread and carries it around the bobbin
Cuts the thread at the end of a seam
review.why: The hook spins around the bobbin, catches the loop that forms behind the rising needle and wraps it around the bobbin thread.

review.q: For a temporary seam that will be pulled out later, what stitch length is best?
review.why: Basting uses a long stitch so the thread slides out easily. Short stitches are hard to remove.

review.q: Dots of bobbin thread appear on the top side of the seam. Which is true?
choices: The top thread is too loose
The top thread is too tight
review.why: Too much top tension drags the bobbin thread up to the surface. Lower the top tension after checking the threading.

review.q: Which of these is the safe way to handle pins while machine sewing?
choices: Pin across the seam and pull each pin out before the foot reaches it
Pin along the seam and sew over them at speed
Leave pins in and remove them all at the end
review.why: Pins set across the seam are easy to pull as the foot approaches. Sewing over a pin can snap the needle.

review.q: The machine stitches unevenly after weeks of use, and it is threaded correctly. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The foot pedal is worn out
Lint under the throat plate and around the bobbin
The stitch width is set too high
review.why: Lint builds up with every seam and interferes with the bobbin thread. Unplug, remove the plate and brush it out.
